title: Eviction-minimizing burst contracts and soft-fallback playbook (PRD WIP)
content:
Purpose

This doc proposes a contract-and-policy layer for Dedicated capacity that minimizes tenant evictions during demand spikes while preserving multi-tenant fairness and predictable economics. The emphasis is on offering burst instruments that: (1) reduce hard evictions, (2) trade latency/cost gracefully, and (3) integrate with existing autoscaler + fallback lanes.

Context / motivation

We've shipped a lot of designs for burst credits, reservoirs, warm pools, and preemptible fallbacks. Common customer feedback: evictions are the single biggest source of outages complaints for Dedicated customers migrating production traffic. Even when fallbacks exist (hosted API, cheaper model variant), abrupt evictions cause request loss and state inconsistencies for LLM apps with long-lived sessions.

Goal(s)
- Reduce tenant-triggered hard evictions by 60% in common microburst scenarios (30–120s spikes).
- Provide fine-grained contractual burst primitives that customers can buy/enable (e.g., grace credits, latency-smoothing, soft-decommit windows).
- Ensure burst behavior is auditable and observable in Console (per-tenant eviction risk, credit burn rate, soft-fallback events).
- Keep economic model simple: burst buys should translate to billable capacity/time credits and clear penalties for overuse.

Non-goals
- Replace existing reserved capacity semantics (we keep reserved capacity as the baseline).
- Solve rare catastrophic cloud failures (AZ down) — those still require region-level failovers.

Key principles
- Prefer graceful degradation over abrupt eviction. When capacity is scarce, degrade across dimensions (latency, concurrency, fidelity) rather than dropping connections.
- Make policies deterministic and predictable for SLO planning. Avoid opaque black-box credit drains.
- Surface actionable telemetry to both customers and ops: why an eviction happened, and what policies could have prevented it.

Core concepts (definitions)
- Soft-fallback: a non-blocking change applied to in-flight or queued requests when capacity pressure is detected, e.g., route to cheaper model variant, lower beam size, or enable output sampling.
- Grace credits: time-limited burst units purchased/allocated to a tenant that allow them to sustain above-reservation throughput without being evicted. Credits burn at measured compute/time rates.
- Decommit window: a short bounded period (configurable per-contract) where the system drains in-progress work and shifts queued requests to fallback lanes before reclaiming GPU resources from a tenant.
- Eviction-minimizing contract (EMC): a product offering bundling grace credits, soft-fallback policies, and SLA-level rules for eviction velocity.

High-level design

1) Contract types
- EMC-basic (free/low-cost trial): small grace credit buffer (e.g., 1–5 minute equivalent at baseline throughput), default soft-fallback rules enabled. No guaranteed headroom.
- EMC-plus (paid): larger credit pool, longer decommit windows (configurable 15–120s), prioritized soft-fallback ordering, and increased telemetry retention for root-cause.
- EMC-enterprise (custom): contractual SLO for eviction rate, dedicated on-call routing, optional pre-warm capacity scheduling for predictable bursts.

2) Runtime policy mixing
- Admission controller checks reservation + current credit balance + global cluster pressure. If request would exceed reservation: (a) if credits available, allow and decrement; (b) if credits exhausted, attempt soft-fallback; (c) if soft-fallback unavailable or unacceptable (customer disallowed some fallbacks), mark request for decommit window/requeue; (d) last resort: eviction.
- Soft-fallbacks are ranked by customer-configured preference and model-aware cost/latency tradeoffs. E.g., model-quantized variant (cheaper), model-shortened-context (lower quality), or proxy-to-hosted API (higher cost).

3) Decommit and graceful drain
- On capacity reclaim events, instead of immediate kill, the system marks tenant slices for decommit and starts a countdown (decommit window). During this window: (i) new requests eligible for soft-fallbacks; (ii) in-progress requests are allowed to finish up to a soft cap (e.g., 30s); (iii) background rebalancer compresses KV caches to speed eviction.
- Operators can choose automatic or operator-acknowledged decommit thresholds.

4) Credit economics
- Credits buy time-equivalent GPU-seconds at a reference profile per model family (we'll publish per-model burn rates). Pricing includes premium for guaranteed non-eviction behavior.
- Credits expire on contract rollovers but can be banked with monthly limits for enterprise customers.

Observability and Console UX

We must add the following views in Console:
- Eviction risk heatmap: per-tenant risk score derived from reserve utilization + credit burn velocity + cluster pressure.
- Credit ledger: live balance, historical burn, cost-to-burn projections.
- Soft-fallback audit trail: timestamped list of fallback events with pre/post SLO impact and sample output for QA.
- Decommit timeline visualizer: shows active decommit windows, queued requests, and reclaim progress.

APIs and config surfaces
- POST /tenants/{id}/emc-purchase -> buy credits, choose contract tier (returns credit id).
- PATCH /tenants/{id}/soft-fallbacks -> configure ordered fallback strategies and per-strategy tolerances (latency cap, quality floor).
- GET /tenants/{id}/eviction-status -> exposures, credit balance, expected time-to-eviction given current burn.
(These are surface proposals; we will iterate with SDK team for shapes.)

Telemetry + SLOs to instrument
- metrics: tenant.credits.balance, tenant.credits.burn_rate, tenant.eviction_attempts, tenant.evict_success, tenant.soft_fallbacks.count, tenant.decommit.windows.started/completed, per-model.burn_rate reference metric.
- alerts: tenant.eviction_attempts > X in 5m, cluster.eviction_ratio > Y, tenant.credit.exhaustion_warning.

Fallback examples (concrete)
- Customer A has a low-latency chat app; prefers latency over fidelity. Soft-fallback order: 1) quantized model variant (latency small increase); 2) reduce max tokens; 3) proxy to hosted variant (expensive) — in that order. Decommit window of 45s.
- Customer B runs embeddings batch jobs and prefers throughput; soft-fallbacks: 1) queue till warm pool available; 2) run on lower-parallelism nodes; 3) fail early with error code + human error remediation link.

Operational playbook (sketch)
- Pre-incident: validate tenant credit purchase and fallback config during onboarding. Simulate microburst scenarios using the load sim harness (ticket: DED-1423).
- During pressure: automated mitigation tries credits -> fallbacks -> decommit. If eviction event occurs, auto-create incident ticket linking telemetry and sample requests.
- Post-incident: run regression eval against the tenant's canonical prompt set; if quality drop observed, recommend refund/credits and adjust contract.

Security/compliance notes
- Soft-fallbacks that involve proxying to hosted models must respect data residency and PII rules. Default policy for customers with data restrictions: soft-fallback to hosted is disabled unless explicitly allowed in EMC-enterprise.

Open questions / risks
- Burn-rate variability: per-request burn depends heavily on prompt length and model variant. How to offer predictable pricing lines without surprising customers? (proposal: publish per-model per-token burn reference + usage estimator in Console).
- Gameability: tenants could intentionally run cheap fallback variants then claim evictions. Need fraud signals (disproportionate fallback churn).
- Complexity: more knobs = customer confusion. Consider opinionated defaults + templates per workload (chat, embeddings, rerank).

Next steps / milestones (rough)
- Nov–Dec: design review with runtime and pricing (owners: Ethan, Marta).
- Jan: prototype admission logic + credit ledger in staging; add minimal console telemetry (owner: Lina).
- Feb: run two pilot customers on EMC-plus; iterate UX.
- Mar: launch EMC-basic self-serve and docs.

Notes to self
- Link experiments from previous warm pool work here: confluence:WARMPOOL-PILOT.
- Coordinate with billing to map credits -> invoice line item.
- Put a simple cost-estimator in the Quickstart for Dedicated customers so they can model credit purchases.

Appendix: quick glossary and sample SLA language (WIP)
- "Eviction rate" = percent of attempted requests that were terminated due to capacity reclaim in a sliding 24h window.
- Sample SLA: "EMC-plus guarantees <= 2% eviction rate attributable to compute shortage during on-contract operation for spikes <= 5x baseline of up to 60s". Draft legal review needed.

----
This is a work-in-progress doc. I want feedback from runtime eng about safe decommit durations and from pricing/billing about how credits should map to GPU-second equivalents. Pinged folks in slack.
